nameStory: The name 'aquatic pygmyweed' tells you everything about this tiny plant's lifestyle and size. 'Pygmy' refers to its diminutive stature - this is one of New England's smallest flowering plants, often less than an inch tall. The 'aquatic' part highlights its love of watery places, from salt marshes to vernal pools.
description: Aquatic pygmyweed is a minuscule succulent plant that's easy to overlook despite its fascinating adaptations. This tiny annual belongs to the stonecrop family and has fleshy, water-storing leaves that help it survive in challenging wetland environments. The entire plant rarely exceeds an inch in height, making it one of New England's most diminutive flowering species. Its small size and preference for muddy, wet areas mean you'll need to look closely to spot this little survivor.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small - the entire plant is typically less than an inch tall, making it easy to miss among other wetland vegetation

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny, thick, and fleshy leaves that feel succulent to the touch, storing water like a miniature jade plant

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small rosettes or mats close to the ground, often partially submerged in shallow water or on wet mud

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Minute white or pinkish flowers that are barely visible to the naked eye, clustered at the plant's center

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Smooth, waxy-feeling surfaces on both stems and leaves that help repel water and retain moisture

habitat: Look for aquatic pygmyweed in salt marshes, the muddy edges of vernal pools, and other wetlands that experience periodic flooding and drying. It thrives in areas that are submerged part of the time but exposed during low water periods, including the muddy banks of estuaries where tides regularly come and go. This plant handles both fresh and slightly salty water, making it adaptable to various coastal and inland wetland environments.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate as water levels recede and muddy surfaces are exposed, with tiny seedlings appearing as small green dots on wet soil.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach their full (though still tiny) size and produce their microscopic flowers during the warmest months when water levels are often at their lowest.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and disperse as autumn rains begin to raise water levels again, preparing for the next generation.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving only seeds to survive the cold months buried in mud or floating in the water.

funFact: Despite being one of New England's tiniest flowering plants, aquatic pygmyweed is actually a succulent related to the popular houseplant jade plant - it's like having a microscopic desert plant that chose to live in a swamp!
confusionNotes: With only 9 recorded observations in New England, you're more likely to overlook it entirely than confuse it with something else. Its tiny size means it might be mistaken for moss or algae, but the fleshy, succulent leaves are the giveaway - moss feels soft and spongy, while pygmyweed feels firm and waxy.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'pygmyweed' is sometimes used for several different tiny aquatic plants, which can cause confusion in field guides. Always check the scientific name Crassula aquatica to be sure you're looking at the right species, as other 'pygmyweeds' belong to entirely different plant families.
compareHints: Aquatic pygmyweed is the only Crassula species commonly found in New England's wetlands. Other stonecrops in the region, like mossy stonecrop, are larger and grow in dry, rocky places rather than wet habitats. While most of its stonecrop relatives prefer well-drained soil and can handle drought, aquatic pygmyweed has gone the opposite direction, adapting its succulent nature to life in waterlogged environments.
